fills.notes: The triadic parallelism is explicit: First Man “sought and found his redeemer”; likewise Mother of Life and Father of the living “sought … this runner” who proceeds from them. The verb-pair ‘sought and found’ maintains the correspondential symmetry (quest → discovery) and keeps the impersonal cosmological register without importing later devotional language.

The sentence enumerates functions of Summons and Obedience: as ‘portals’ they also become ‘helpers … of the First Man’. In the oldest cosmological register, these are not moral acts but operative forces; pairing ‘helpers and powers’ is a common correspondential collocation (aid as effect; power as potency).

What they ‘gave him’ during ascent should be interior provisions corresponding to restoration of the Living Soul: memory (remembrance of origin) and force (strength for separation from Death). This matches the next lines where they are ‘bestowers of remembrance’ and ‘purifiers’.

They “gave him … the Father of Life and the Mother of Life …” fits an infinitival purpose: enabling encounter/approach to the higher sources. ‘To meet’ preserves the structural, non-hagiographic tone (not ‘to worship’, ‘to pray’).

The clause contrasts locations/states where the living soul is embedded: ‘in … in the tree or in the creation of flesh …’. In the substrate cosmology the three common natural repositories are waters, vegetation (tree), and flesh (animal/human). Thus ‘waters’ completes a triad of ultimates (fluid/vegetative/animal) for purification and recollection.

After ‘creation of flesh’ the correspondential extension is to embodiment generally: flesh as the general natural formation, ‘every body’ as its varied ultimates. This keeps the teaching impersonal and comprehensive (no later ethical/pastoral turn).

assessment: Most gaps can be constrained by the text’s internal correspondential parallelism: summons/obedience function as operative ‘portals’, giving remembrance and strength, enabling ascent and reunion with the higher living sources, and acting upon the soul across its natural repositories (waters/tree/flesh/body). Exact wording is tightest where the chapter itself provides a model phrase (‘sought and found’); looser where the lacuna likely held a short purpose-clause or a concluding generalizer.
